name: source-map (wasm-mappings SourceMapConsumer)
baseline: source-map 0.6.x pure-JavaScript SourceMapConsumer (the previous implementation of the same library)
workload: Parsing source maps and querying mappings through SourceMapConsumer, with the hot paths rewritten in Rust and compiled to WebAssembly (lib/mappings.wasm).
claimed_speedup: up to 5.89x faster than the JavaScript implementation on realistic benchmarks (Mozilla Hacks post, figure seen in a search-result snippet only); CHANGELOG 0.7.0 says SourceMapConsumer 'now uses WebAssembly, and is much faster', 0.7.2 says 'Another 3x speed up in SourceMapConsumer' (no numbers)
stars_or_usage: 3.7k stars; widely used JavaScript tooling dependency
tradeoffs: API became asynchronous in 0.7 (new SourceMapConsumer returns a Promise) and consumers must call destroy() to free manually managed wasm memory; the wasm file must be located and loaded by the host (initialize() with a URL or ArrayBuffer in browsers).
caveats: The Mozilla Hacks post was unreachable from this environment (host not resolvable), so the 5.89x figure comes from a WebSearch result snippet only and was not checked against the post; no benchmark code was opened. The CHANGELOG (opened on github.com/mozilla/source-map) only says 'much faster'. 0.7.2 attributes a further 3x to a follow-up post titled 'Speed without wizardry' (not opened), so how much of the final gain comes from wasm rather than JS-side tuning is unclear. Numbers date from January 2018.
found_via: WebSearch 'WebAssembly library ... times faster than pure JavaScript' surfaced the Mozilla Hacks post title and snippet; then opened github.com/mozilla/source-map README, CHANGELOG.md and package.json, and github.com/fitzgen/source-map-mappings

name: js-angusj-clipper
language: C++ (Clipper) compiled to WebAssembly/asm.js, TypeScript API
baseline: jsclipper (pure-JavaScript port of Angus Johnson's Clipper) and the library's own asm.js build
workload: Polygon boolean operations (intersection, union, difference, xor) and offsetting over circle polygons, e.g. 500 operations over two 5000-point circles and 10000 operations over two 100-point circles.
claimed_speedup: boolean ops on moderately big polygons: wasm ~0.4 s vs pure JS ~1.0 s (README summary); e.g. 500 intersections of two 5000-point circles 212 ms wasm vs 573 ms pure JS vs 598 ms asm.js; 100 miter offsets of a 5000-point circle (delta 5) 129 ms wasm vs 702 ms pure JS. Small polygons: ~0.7 s vs ~1.0 s
compiler_and_flags: Emscripten build (flags not stated in README)
tradeoffs: Data is copied across the JS/wasm boundary on every call, so small polygons gain less; asm.js fallback is no faster than pure JS because 64-bit integers are emulated; Boost-style Clipper1 API (Clipper2 supersedes it).
caveats: First-party numbers from the test suite on an unnamed machine under Node, not in a browser. The same-library-natively baseline is not measured. Original C++ Clipper is a separate catalogued project (polyclipping).
found_via: Candidate recalled by name and confirmed by the Clipper2-WASM README, which names this repo as its Clipper1 WASM baseline; opened the repo README, package.json and github.com pages

name: Clipper2-WASM (clipper2-wasm)
language: C++ (Clipper2) compiled to WebAssembly, JavaScript/TypeScript API
workload: Boolean operations (intersection, union, difference, xor) over two intersecting circle paths of 5,000 points each, repeated 5,000 times in the browser benchmark page.
claimed_speedup: README screenshot of the benchmark page: intersection 1962.1 ms (Clipper1) vs 1163.3 ms (Clipper2), +40.71%; union 2434.2 vs 1817.4 ms, +25.34%; difference 2122.5 vs 1472.8 ms, +30.61%; xor 2609.0 vs 2278.4 ms, +12.67%
hardware: Apple M2 Pro (from the README heading); browser not stated
tradeoffs: Wasm module must be loaded and instantiated before use; objects created on the wasm side need explicit delete().
caveats: The numbers exist only as a PNG screenshot in the README; I downloaded and read the image. The comparison is Clipper2 against Clipper1, both as wasm, so the gain is mostly algorithmic and not wasm versus JS. The harness is public in clipper2-wasm/examples/benchmark (clipper1-vs-clipper2.html, testPolyOperation.js). Build flags and the browser are not stated. Clipper2 itself (C++) is a separate project.
found_via: Candidate recalled by name; opened github.com/ErikSom/Clipper2-WASM, read the README, the benchmark example sources via raw.githubusercontent.com and the README benchmark image

name: blake3 (Node.js and browser, WebAssembly build)
language: Rust (WebAssembly and native bindings) with TypeScript wrapper
baseline: Node.js built-in crypto md5, sha1 and sha256; also the library's own native binding
workload: Hashing 64 B, 64 KB and 6 MB buffers, measured in ops/sec with matcha on Node 12.
claimed_speedup: 64 B: blake3 wasm 1,040,000 ops/sec vs sha256 271,000 (about 3.8x, derived from page data) and native binding 625,000; 64 KB: wasm 6,470 sha256 vs 6,410 blake3 wasm (parity), native 48,900; 6 MB: sha256 69.2 vs blake3 wasm 65.2 vs native 502
tradeoffs: WebAssembly build is much slower than the native binding on large inputs (6 MB: 65 vs 502 ops/sec) and roughly equal to sha256 above 64 KB.
caveats: Wasm beats the same library compiled natively only on tiny inputs (64 B) where call overhead dominates; on large buffers it does not beat Node's built-in sha256. README says native bindings were a work in progress when measured; numbers are from Node 12 on an unnamed MacBook. Last commit 2022-10-09 (v3.0.0).
found_via: Candidate recalled by name (wasm hash libraries); read the README Speed section via raw.githubusercontent.com and the github.com repo and commits pages

language: C++ (mcl/bls) compiled to WebAssembly, JavaScript API
baseline: noble-bls12-381 (pure JavaScript); blst native bindings shown for reference
workload: BLS12-381 signature operations (sign, verify, aggregate, verifyMultiple) through the ChainSafe/bls wrapper, in ops/sec.
claimed_speedup: verify: herumi wasm 47.674 ops/s vs noble JS 17.906 (about 2.7x, derived) vs blst native 326.38; sign: 108.81 vs 10.246 (about 10.6x, derived) vs blst 925.49; aggregate pubkeys (30): 2898.9 vs 1875.0 vs blst 15686

The wasm library is compared with a pure-JS implementation, not with the same library compiled natively.
found_via: Candidate recalled by name; read the ChainSafe/bls README Benchmarks section via raw.githubusercontent.com, and opened github.com/herumi/bls-eth-wasm for license and commits

name: BlazeDiff core-wasm (@blazediff/core-wasm)
language: Rust (wasm32 with simd128) with JavaScript wrapper
workload: Pixel-by-pixel perceptual (YIQ) diff of pre-decoded RGBA buffers over 4K, blazediff, page and pixelmatch fixtures, 25 iterations after 5 warmups, image decode excluded.
claimed_speedup: about 50.8% average improvement over pixelmatch; e.g. 4k/1 332.26 ms pixelmatch vs 33.18 ms core-wasm (90.0%, about 10x), blazediff/1 1.24 ms vs 0.24 ms; identical-image 4k/2 22.70 ms vs 22.17 ms (2.3%)
compiler_and_flags: Rust to wasm32-unknown-unknown with +simd128 (v128 SIMD), per README; rustc version not stated
hardware: Apple M1 Max, Node.js 22 (BENCHMARKS.md hardware specifications)
tradeoffs: Counts agree with pixelmatch to within about 0.05% on the fixtures, so results are not bit-identical (different edge-case handling); requires wasm SIMD (v128).
caveats: Benchmark harness is public in the repo (npm benchmark scripts and benchmarks/ folder), but I did not run it. The package README says up to ~16x on 4K while the benchmark page shows about 10x for 4k/1; I quoted the benchmark page. Same author as the pixelmatch-compatible JS core and the Rust native build; the wasm build is slower than the native binary. First-party.
found_via: npm registry search (queries 'webassembly faster than javascript', 'wasm faster than js', 'wasm times faster', 'webassembly simd fast') found @blazediff/core-wasm; opened github.com/teimurjan/blazediff README, BENCHMARKS.md and benchmarks/pixel-by-pixel.md

name: sparkdown (@momiji-rs/sparkdown, WebAssembly build)
language: Rust (wasm32 with simd128 and bulk-memory) with JavaScript wrapper
baseline: remark-parse (mdast-util-from-markdown, JavaScript) and the native pulldown-cmark crate
workload: Parsing the 200 KB CommonMark spec document to an mdast tree (fully materialised plain objects) and rendering it to HTML, measured in Node on one machine.
claimed_speedup: toMdast({position:false}) about 0.9 ms vs remark about 73 ms (about 80x); wasm HTML render 0.93 ms vs native pulldown-cmark 0.68 ms and cmark about 1.9 ms
compiler_and_flags: RUSTFLAGS='-C target-feature=+simd128,+bulk-memory' cargo build --release --features wasm --target wasm32-unknown-unknown
hardware: Apple Mac Studio (chip not stated), Node
stars_or_usage: 3 stars; about 46k npm downloads per month
tradeoffs: Wasm build is about 1.4x slower than sparkdown's own native build (0.93 vs 0.59 ms) and slower than native pulldown-cmark on HTML rendering; the mdast path crosses the wasm boundary as a binary wire format.
caveats: First-party, one machine, best-of-15, CPU model unspecified; the roughly 80x figure compares parsing to an mdast tree with remark, not HTML rendering. The in-repo cargo bench only covers sparkdown versus pulldown-cmark; the remark comparison lives in harness/. Very young project (v0.1.0, June 2026, 3 stars).

name: zaw (Zero-Allocation WASM)
language: Zig and Rust (WebAssembly) with TypeScript host
baseline: Plain JavaScript loop and Rust wasm-bindgen
workload: XOR of a scalar into an Int32Array passed in and out of WebAssembly, for 10 to 100,000 elements, measured with vitest bench.
claimed_speedup: vs JavaScript: 6.0x at 100 elements, 11.4x at 1,000, 12.8x at 10,000, 13.8x at 100,000; vs wasm-bindgen 6.2x, 6.9x, 3.3x, 4.3x; at 10 elements plain JS is 1.6x faster than zaw
compiler_and_flags: Zig 0.16.0 and Rust (per CI badges); flags not checked
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D 16-Core Processor (docs/benchmarks.md); Node/browser version not stated
tradeoffs: It is an interop protocol, not an algorithm library; wins only when data is large enough to amortise the call (not at 10 elements) and the author picks the cheapest possible kernel to expose interop cost.
caveats: The benchmark is a deliberate micro-benchmark (XOR of Int32Array) chosen to show interop overhead; the author argues it is representative. First-party numbers, but the raw vitest output with CPU model is in the repo. I did not check build flags or the host runtime, so the tier is C rather than A. The 'Transfer In Float64Array' benchmark in the same file shows wasm-bindgen faster than zaw.
found_via: npm registry search (queries 'webassembly faster than javascript', 'wasm faster than js', 'wasm times faster', 'webassembly simd fast') found the npm package zaw; opened github.com/stylearcade/zaw README and docs/benchmarks.md

name: kmeans-wasm
language: Rust (WebAssembly SIMD, simd128) with JavaScript wrapper
workload: k-means clustering of random RGB pixels, random multi-dimensional points and four real photographs for colour quantisation; median of five runs.
claimed_speedup: 10,000 points x 50 dims x 10 clusters 83.15 ms vs skmeans 1456.35 ms (17.5x); 100,000 random RGB pixels, 32 colours 247.03 vs 1677.87 ms (6.8x); photo blue-marble, 16 colours 109.24 vs 11133.62 ms (101.8x); small input 1,000 pixels, 2 colours 0.47 vs 0.41 ms (0.9x, slower)
compiler_and_flags: Rust compiled to wasm with simd128 (README); rustc version and exact flags not stated in README
tradeoffs: Requires wasm SIMD (Chrome 91+, Firefox 89+, Safari 16.4+); small inputs and tiny cluster counts gain little or lose.
caveats: Large part of the image speed-ups comes from an algorithmic change (collapsing the image to its distinct colours and weighting them), not from wasm alone; the README says the speed-up falls from 84x to 13x as distinct colours grow. Benchmark harness (js_bench folder and benches) is public but I did not run it; tier A rests on the README's stated CPU, runtime and median-of-five method plus public harness, with build flags only partly stated. First-party.
found_via: npm registry search (queries 'webassembly faster than javascript', 'webassembly simd fast', 'wasm parser') then github.com/vusolapohvistr/kmeans-wasm README Benchmarks section and commits page

name: wasm-fast-compress (@addmaple/gzip, lz4, brotli)
language: Rust (WebAssembly with simd128; flate2 with zlib-rs, lz4_flex fork, rust-brotli fork)
baseline: pako (gzip), lz4js (lz4) and the brotli npm package (README calls it both a JS port and Google's C implementation)
workload: Compressing a 1.28 MB JSON file in Node on an M4 Mac, median time per call at several levels.
claimed_speedup: gzip vs pako: level 1 about 3.8 ms vs 14 ms (3.7x), level 6 7.0 vs 22 ms (3.1x), level 9 11.7 vs 58 ms (5.0x); lz4 vs lz4js about 1.4 vs 4.0 ms (2.9x); brotli level 9 36 vs 48.6 ms (1.35x) and level 11 about 30 ms vs 2.7 s (about 90x)
compiler_and_flags: SIMD build with -C target-feature=+simd128 (README); base build without simd128
tradeoffs: docs/PERFORMANCE_NOTES.md says that for inputs under 50 KB JS libraries are often faster (2-28x) because of copying at the JS-wasm boundary, mixed at 50-500 KB; the non-SIMD wasm brotli build is about 4x slower than native.
caveats: The brotli level 11 result (about 90x) is implausible and is probably a level or window mismatch between libraries, so treat it as unverified (cap at C). The README names the brotli baseline as a JS port in one table and as Google's native C in the performance text. One input file, one machine. The benchmarks/ folder exists in the repo but I did not read it. Output is not claimed to be byte-identical to pako or zlib.
found_via: WebSearch 'WebAssembly gzip OR zlib ... faster than pako' and then npm registry search (query 'simd128') found @addmaple/lz4 and @addmaple/gzip; opened github.com/addmaple/wasm-fast-compress README and docs/PERFORMANCE_NOTES.md
